name: Yvette Violet
lede: Yvette Violet is a dark, greyed violet-purple recorded by Ridgway in 1912; who Yvette was is undocumented in the sources we hold.

sections.title: A violet with a woman's name
sections.body:
The library dates Yvette Violet to Ridgway's 1912 color chart, plate XXXVI, hue 55′′, tone k, and to the ISCC-NBS block 228 of 1955 [1]. Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary lists it too, first recorded in 1912, the same year as Ridgway's plate [1]. None of our sources explain who Yvette was, so the name's origin is undocumented here [1].

In LCH terms it measures lightness 36, chroma 16, hue 304 degrees, a dark, muted violet [1]. The nearest named colors on file are [[dusky-violet]], [[del-monte]], [[dusty-purple-tone]] and [[dark-madder-violet]], at 3, 3.2, 4.5 and 5 ΔE [1]. Closer kin by name alone are [[violet]], [[mauve]] and [[grape]] [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds a close match to Yvette Violet in 55 of 23,781 paintings, about 0.23 percent, as photographed [2]. The earliest dated match is Taddeo di Bartolo's The Crucifixion, from 1401, five centuries before the name was recorded, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [2]. It peaks in the 1900s, in 8 of 1,674 paintings, at 5.3 times the archive's overall rate for that century, and John Singer Sargent carries it in three of his 287 paintings here [2]. Inside a painting it most often sits in shadow, in 60 percent of its appearances [2].

origin.named_after: undocumented; a woman's first name, per Ridgway 1912
